title: Developing Vocational Paths for Every Kind of Kid in the House
author: Michael Foster
summary: Foster addresses the false choice between college or trades, arguing parents should help children discover individual vocations based on gifts rather than forcing uniform paths. He advocates a household guild model with apprenticeships, internships, and on-the-job training. The piece emphasizes avoiding crushing student debt while maintaining academic rigor. Foster argues against anti-education pendulum swings and advocates sober, vocation-focused education decisions. Core theme: competence, character, and direction matter more than rigid college or no-college ideologies.
points: Household operates like small guild: identify gifts, provide training, build connections
Avoid false choice between college vs. trades; focus on competence and vocation-fitness
Wise education approach weights cost, student formation, and long-term usefulness
Daughters can pursue college if financially prudent and spiritually sound
Parents must take responsibility for children's formation and job placement
quotes: I am not interested in pushing them all down the same path. I am interested in helping them become competent adults who can shoulder responsibility and serve somewhere real.

The trades are good and necessary. A disciplined young plumber or electrician with a bit of business sense will do very well. But a healthy society also needs teachers and lawyers and judges and engineers.

The household should function like a small guild. Identify gifts. Provide training. Build connections. Help them step into the world with skill and confidence. This used to be normal. It can be normal again if we are willing to take responsibility for the formation and placement of our own children.
A wise approach weighs the cost, the formation of the student, and the long term usefulness of the degree. It is possible to pursue serious education without surrendering convictions or common sense.
In short, the goal is not college or no college. The goal is competence, character, and direction.” Archived from This is Foster on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
